intro: Kinshasa is not waiting for a school operating system. It already has one: cash at the gate, a register in a drawer, a WhatsApp group that never ends, and a bursar who reconciles after the term has already leaked.

That system has a price. In this city, most primary schools are private — they run on parent fees, not a ministry payroll. When balances live in three places, the school finances the gap. When parents only learn a balance at the gate, collections slip. When report cards are rebuilt from chats, the office shuts down for a week.

ShuleOS was built in Kinshasa for that reality: Programme National, French first, CDF and USD, mobile money, WhatsApp, attendance that survives a dead signal. The next term does not have to buy the same leaks again.

sections.title: Kinshasa is a private-school city. Fees are the operating budget.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa neighbourhood with private school courtyards, uniforms, and motorcycle taxis at the end of the school day.
sections.imageCaption: Kinshasa is the exception in the DRC: most primary schools here are private. Parent fees are not a side account — they are how the school runs.
body: Nationally, private schools are about 17% of the system. Kinshasa is not the nation. The ministry's own yearbook put private primary schools at 66.4% of all primary schools in this city. Haut-Katanga is the other outlier. Everywhere else, the mix looks different.

That number is the whole argument. A Kinshasa private school does not "also collect fees." It lives on them — teacher pay, chalk, fuel for the generator, the next intake campaign. Research on low-income Kinshasa neighbourhoods found private fees ranging from about $8 a year to several hundred. Elite schools publish in the thousands of dollars. The ministry does not set those prices. Your bursar is the system of record — or there isn't one.

When the record is a notebook, the school is already paying: disputed balances, families who leave because nobody could answer, cash that never quite matches the register. That is not a software wish. It is this year's budget walking out the gate.
sections.cost: A private school with no single fee ledger is financing its own leaks. Every "we'll check" is money that should have been on the books this week.
sections.fix: One student account tied to fee structures, invoices, payments, and history — so the bursar, the director, and the parent are looking at the same balance.
sections.who: School owners and directors in Kinshasa whose entire year depends on collections they can actually see.

sections.title: Cash, CDF, USD, and "we'll check" is how money disappears.
sections.imageAlt: A bursar desk in Kinshasa with handwritten fee registers, mixed CDF and USD notes, and a phone showing a digital invoice.
sections.imageCaption: Parents already pay how Kinshasa pays: cash, CDF, USD, and mobile money. The leak is the school that cannot show the exact balance — or prove the receipt.
body: Kinshasa parents do not wait for a bank appointment to pay school. They pay in Congolese francs, in dollars, in cash at the window, and increasingly on the phone. Mobile money is no longer a side channel. In 2025 the telecom regulator's figures put M-Pesa and Airtel Money in the same league — hundreds of millions of dollars in service revenue — the kind of number you only see when a payment rail has become infrastructure.

The University of Kinshasa opened mobile payment for academic fees in 2025 for a reason it said out loud: cut the queues, and fight fake receipts. If UNIKIN is still fighting faux reçus, so is every private school stamping carbon copies at the gate.
A foreign school tool that invoices in one currency, with no mobile-money path and no WhatsApp reminder, asks your bursar to keep a second system. That second system is where the leaks live.
sections.cost: Balances in three places. Parents disputing at the gate. Collections that look fine until someone reconciles — too late to recover the term.
sections.fix: Fee structures by class, term, or boarding. Invoices with history. CDF and USD. Mobile-money-ready amounts. WhatsApp reminders before the due date — not after the queue forms. Expenses, payroll, and reports beside the same ledger.
sections.who: Bursars who should not spend Sunday reconstructing what was paid in cash, on the phone, and "to the teacher."

sections.title: Parents already have a portal. It's WhatsApp. It has no ledger.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa parent checking a school portal on her phone at home, with an office queue faded in the background.
sections.imageCaption: The office queue is the old portal. The phone is where Kinshasa parents already live — they just cannot see the real balance, the absence, or the grade until it is costly.
body: Ask a Kinshasa parent how they talk to the school. The answer is almost never "the parent portal." It is a class WhatsApp group, a director's personal number, and a trip to the secretariat when the chat goes silent. That is communication. It is not a record.

Unlogged chats become disputes with no proof. "Come to the office" becomes the default reply — and every visit costs staff time, parent time, and often a delayed payment. Trust erodes when the fee figure and the grade arrive late, or wrong.

Most Congolese parents already manage school life from a phone. Without a real portal, they miss balances, grades, and absences until the queue or a crisis. You pay in trust, in time, and in fees that land after the reminder should have gone out.
sections.cost: The secretariat becomes a helpdesk. Teachers repeat the same update twenty times. Parents find out by accident — and then they don't pay, or they don't come back.
sections.fix: A parent portal for performance, fees, timetable, messages, and events. A student portal for assignments, grades, library, and timetable. Mass WhatsApp, SMS, and in-app outreach with a trail — so the school can prove what was said.
sections.who: Parents who should not travel across Kinshasa for a balance; offices that should not be a call centre every fee week.

sections.title: Programme National bulletins cannot be an all-nighter.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa teacher at night surrounded by paper report cards, with a laptop showing a clean digital bulletin.
sections.imageCaption: Report-card week is not a printing problem. It is the bill for a term of grades that lived in registers, chats, and memory.
body: The Congolese school year runs roughly September to July. The bulletin is not a US-style GPA export. Teachers are expected to report against Programme National learning areas, term by term, in a format families and inspectors recognise. When grades live in a register, a chat, and a personal spreadsheet, that format gets rebuilt by hand — usually at night, usually with errors that become parent fights.

Foreign student-information systems fail here in a boring way: they assume a different report card, a different year, a different language of work. Staff then keep a paper parallel. The parallel is what shuts the office down.
ShuleOS keeps attendance, the gradebook, assignments, exams, and Programme National report cards in the teacher workflow. The term should end with printable cards, not a scramble.
sections.cost: Evenings gone. Printing week as an all-nighter. Errors that turn into meetings. Academic records nobody would sign if they had to defend them in October.
sections.fix: Classes and sections aligned to DRC grade levels. Daily attendance. Gradebooks and exams mapped to national curriculum strands. Report cards that come out of the same file the teacher already used all term.
sections.who: Teachers who want evenings back; pedagogy leads who need the same bulletin logic across every class.

sections.title: Attendance that dies with the signal is attendance you invented.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa teacher marking attendance on a smartphone in class while a router light sits dark in the corner.
sections.imageCaption: Nationwide, most people are still offline. In Kinshasa the signal is better — until it isn't. The roll call cannot wait for Vodacom.
body: At the end of 2025, about 34.7 million people in the DRC used the internet — 30.5% of the population. There were 64.7 million mobile connections, many of them voice-only. Kinshasa is an island of coverage compared with the interior. It is still an island that blinks.

A classroom with a dead connection does not pause the day. Teachers fall back to paper, then double-enter at night — if they remember, if the list survived the bag. Directors then make decisions on reconstructed guesses: who is chronically absent, which class is emptying, whether the fee reminder should have gone to that family.
ShuleOS installs on the phone like an app. Attendance keeps working offline and syncs when the signal returns. The day still counts.
sections.cost: Ghost rolls. Night-time re-entry. Absences parents hear about when it is already a discipline meeting — or a lost fee.
sections.fix: An installable PWA, no special hardware. Bulk marking, absence alerts, and offline sync — so the register is the same object the director reads later.
sections.who: Teachers in rooms where connectivity is optional; directors who need real attendance, not a reconstructed week.

sections.title: The next intake decides on a phone, not at your gate.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa family on the sidewalk looking at a school website on a phone, with a torn paper admissions notice on the wall behind them.
sections.imageCaption: Families search WhatsApp and Google before they visit. A school with no site is asking them to find the competitor first.
body: Kinshasa has no shortage of private schools. That is the point: families choose. They ask in WhatsApp groups. They search. They judge the first screen. A school with no professional site, and admissions on paper that get lost in a drawer, is not "traditional." It is invisible at the exact moment a parent is ready to enroll.
Paper admissions mean delays, incomplete files, and families who never finish. Every intake season without a site, some of those families choose the school they found first.
ShuleOS includes a branded public website — homepage, admissions, events, hiring, school-visit booking — feeding straight into the admin queue. Interest becomes a file, not a maybe.
sections.cost: Empty seats you will still staff. Forms that vanish. A first impression that looks like 2012 while the school next door looks open.
sections.fix: A free branded site with your colours and cover image. Online admissions into the same academic core. Events, careers listings, and visit booking without a second tool.
sections.who: Directors competing for families who decide on a phone screen in Gombe, Lemba, or Ngaliema — not in your courtyard.

sections.title: Directors shouldn't find out in July what broke in October.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa school director at dusk looking at a live dashboard, with unused ledgers stacked beside the screen.
sections.imageCaption: By the time the spreadsheet is "done," the term is over. The expensive problems — empty seats, unpaid fees, silent absences — were visible in week three.
body: A Kinshasa director is already running a business, a ministry-facing school, and a community. The information to do that job exists. It is just late. Attendance in one book, fees in another, grades in a third, branch numbers in a WhatsApp forward. By the time someone types it into a spreadsheet, the term has moved on.
That delay has a shape: a class that emptied in October, a collection shortfall that was obvious in November, a teacher whose register never matched. You cannot hire, chase, or intervene in July.
ShuleOS puts students, attendance, finance, and branch performance on dashboards leadership can read in minutes — exportable for a board or an inspection, not rebuilt for one.
sections.cost: Decisions made blind. Reports that take a week. Multi-campus operators reconciling five versions of the truth.
sections.fix: Executive dashboards, attendance heatmaps, collection rates, academic trends, branch comparison — the view you needed in October.
sections.who: Principals and multi-branch owners who should not wait for a bursar's Sunday spreadsheet to know if the school is healthy.

sections.title: Foreign SIS tools fail here. This one was built on Batetela.
sections.imageAlt: A Kinshasa high-rise office at dusk, Congolese support staff on laptops and phones helping a school, city skyline in the windows.
sections.imageCaption: Support that keeps Kinshasa hours, speaks French first, and already knows what a bulletin and a mobile-money receipt look like.
body: Tools built for other systems ignore the things that are not optional here: Programme National report cards, CDF and USD in the same week, French-first staff, WhatsApp-heavy parents, classrooms where the internet is a guest. You can translate the menus. You cannot translate the workflow. Staff keep the paper parallel, and you have paid for two systems.

ShuleOS is a product of Digni Digital LLC, based at Crown Towers on Batetela, 15th floor, Kinshasa. Support runs Monday to Friday, 8:00 to 18:00 WAT, on WhatsApp and email — the same channels the school already uses. Onboarding is four steps, most of it in an afternoon: register, launch the public site, invite every role, open the portals.
No setup fees. No special hardware. The school you already run, in one place that does not forget.
sections.cost: Another year bending foreign software until it almost fits — while the real school still lives in notebooks.
sections.fix: French and English. Local fee and curriculum workflows. WhatsApp-native reminders. Mobile money. Offline attendance. Roles and audit logs. Support from the same city as the school.
sections.who: Kinshasa schools tired of importing a system that was never asked to survive this city.
